analysis.one_liner: Froze nearly all new federal regulations for two years.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in two House committees without a vote and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred federal agencies from issuing, amending, or repealing regulations for two years, with narrow exceptions for emergencies, criminal enforcement, civil rights rules (not counting quotas or preferences), foreign affairs, and aviation safety. Agencies would also have had to file detailed cost-benefit and employment-impact statements before making any new rules after the freeze. The bill was referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary committees, then to subcommittees, and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries subject to federal regulation gain the most: every rule touching workplace safety, air and water pollution, food safety, consumer finance, and similar matters would be delayed for two years, postponing compliance costs. Supporters argued businesses needed the break from new rules to hire and invest.

how_it_helps.text: Bars every federal agency from any rulemaking action for a two-year period beginning 30 days after enactment, unless an exception applies.
Extends any legal deadline tied to rulemaking for five months or until the end of the moratorium, whichever is later, postponing obligations that depended on new rules.

Requires each agency to prepare economic impact statements — certified by OMB — estimating costs, benefits, and employment effects for all rules pending when the freeze began, and for any rule considered afterward.

Carves out exceptions for imminent health or safety threats (requiring OIRA approval), criminal-law enforcement, anti-discrimination rules other than quotas or preferences, military and foreign affairs functions other than procurement, and aviation safety.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people bear the cost: two years of delayed protections — new air and water pollution limits, workplace and product safety updates, food safety rules, and consumer financial protections would all be postponed. Workers waiting on court-ordered or statutory deadlines tied to regulations would wait longer.

drawbacks.text: The two-year freeze would delay new public protections across health, safety, environment, and finance, since any rule not fitting a narrow exception would be barred even if its benefits clearly outweighed its costs.

Getting an emergency waiver requires written approval from the Administrator of OIRA within OMB and publication in the Federal Register, adding a political gate in front of urgent health and safety rules.
Extending deadlines for actions that depended on rulemaking could push back court-ordered and statutory obligations for up to the full two-year period.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A two-year blanket moratorium goes far beyond targeted regulatory relief. It treats health, safety, environmental, and financial rules the same regardless of their merits, and the emergency exceptions are narrow and require OIRA sign-off. Some industries would have saved compliance costs for two years, but the public would bear delayed protections and postponed deadlines across the board.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, but no committee ever voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Reid Ribble introduced the bill on March 31, 2011, and it was referred to the Committees on Oversight and Government Reform and the Judiciary.

In April 2011 it was referred to a subcommittee on regulatory affairs within one committee and, in August 2011, to a courts and administrative law subcommittee in the other; neither took further action.
Twenty-four House Republicans cosponsored the bill, all from one party, and no Senate companion action appears in the record.
The bill received no markup, no floor vote, and no action in the Senate before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and financial protections are better off, since the proposed two-year freeze never advanced. Industries waiting out new rules did not get the pause they sought from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Reid Ribble
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral, passed it to a regulatory affairs subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral, passed it to a courts and administrative law subcommittee, and never scheduled a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrats are listed as supporting the bill, and it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have postponed every new regulation these industries face for two years, cutting their near-term compliance costs. The public would have borne the cost as delayed health, safety, environmental, and financial protections.

Agencies would have been barred from rulemaking and required to produce certified economic impact statements for all pending and future rules, sharply limiting their ability to carry out statutory mandates on schedule.
